Every design we've analyzed in Sections 1-7 has had a single random-sampling unit:
participants. But in a wide range of rehabilitation research, the measurement *instrument*
itself is also a sample from a larger population, not fixed and exhaustively enumerated. Two
examples that come up constantly:

* In **speech-language pathology**, a confrontation-naming or word-reading task presents
  participants with some number of specific words (or pictures to be named). Those particular
  words are a sample from a much larger population of possible words you could have used to
  test the same underlying ability, in exactly the same sense that your participants are a
  sample from a larger population of possible participants.
* In **health-professions education** (e.g., a DPT program's written exams or OSCEs), a given
  test is made up of some number of specific items. Those items are themselves a sample from a
  much larger population of possible questions you could have written to assess the same competency -
  a different cohort's exam, covering the identical learning objectives, would use different
  wording and different specific scenarios.

The companion paper for this repository already introduced this idea directly, in almost
exactly the speech-pathology framing above (see "Variation in Multiple Crossed Factors,"
which models a linguistic word-recognition experiment with random intercepts for both
`subject` and `stimulus`). This section builds that idea out into a full worked example set in
a "confrontation-naming" task, so named because a participant is "confronted" with a 
specific stimulus and is asked to name it (e.g., the Boston Naming Task). 
Crossed designs like this come up often enough - and are confusing enough - to 
deserve an expanded treatment. Everything here applies just as directly to the
DPT-assessment scenario with random effects like (`(1|student) + (1|item)` 
in place of `(1|participant) + (1|word)`), and we come back to that parallel 
at the end of the section.

## 1. Nested vs. Crossed Random Effects (A Quick Refresher)

We introduced nested and crossed random effects back in Section 3:

* **Fully Nested**: every level of one factor belongs to exactly one level of another (e.g., a
  patient belongs to exactly one clinic).
* **Fully Crossed**: every level of one factor is paired with every level of another (e.g., every
  participant responds to every word).

When participants and items are fully crossed and you ignore the item side of that structure
- either by treating items as fixed effects, or (worse) by averaging over them - you commit
what Clark (1973) named **the language-as-fixed-effect fallacy**. Despite the name, this is not
only a linguistics problem: it applies exactly the same way to a DPT exam with a specific bank
of items, or a balance-assessment protocol built from a specific set of perturbation trials.
Treating a random sample of items as if it exhausted the population you actually care about
inflates your false-positive rate, sometimes dramatically - simulations in this literature
(e.g., Judd, Westfall, & Yarkoni, 2012) have shown nominal 5% error rates climbing as high as
30-50% once you have a reasonably-sized bank of items and ignore the variability between them.

## 2. Simulating a Crossed Design: Confrontation Naming in Aphasia

Consider a confrontation-naming study: 32 people with aphasia are each asked to name 40
pictured objects, and every participant attempts every picture (a fully crossed design). Half
of the pictures have high-frequency names (e.g., "dog", "chair") and half have low-frequency
names (e.g., "anchor", "trellis"). Word frequency is one of the most robustly replicated
predictors of naming performance in the aphasiology literature, so it's a reasonable fixed effect
of interest. The outcome is naming latency, in milliseconds, on trials the participant names
correctly.

```{r libraries, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
```

```{r simulate-crossed-data}
set.seed(789)
n_participants <- 32   # people with aphasia
n_words        <- 40   # pictured items, sampled from a much larger pool of nameable objects

df_crossed <- expand.grid(
  participant = factor(paste0("P", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_participants))),
  word        = factor(paste0("W", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_words)))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Because expand.grid() here varies `participant` fastest, splitting frequency by
    # as.numeric(word) correctly assigns each WORD to exactly one frequency category
    # (a given picture's name is always High- or Low-frequency, consistently,
    # across every participant who sees it), unlike splitting by row order.
    frequency = factor(if_else(as.numeric(word) <= (n_words / 2), "High", "Low"),
                        levels = c("High", "Low"))
  )

# Random effects for participants and words
p_intercepts <- rnorm(n_participants, mean = 0, sd = 300)
names(p_intercepts) <- levels(df_crossed$participant)

w_intercepts <- rnorm(n_words, mean = 0, sd = 150)
names(w_intercepts) <- levels(df_crossed$word)

# Random slope for frequency within participants (people with aphasia vary in how much
# a low-frequency name costs them, beyond the average frequency effect)
p_slopes <- rnorm(n_participants, mean = 0, sd = 90)
names(p_slopes) <- levels(df_crossed$participant)

df_crossed <- df_crossed %>%
  mutate(
    naming_latency = 1500 +
      220 * (frequency == "Low") +
      p_intercepts[participant] +
      w_intercepts[word] +
      p_slopes[participant] * (frequency == "Low") +
      rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = 150)
  )
```

## 3. Model Specification Comparison: What Happens if We Ignore Item Variance?

```{r fit-three-models}
# Model A: Incorrect - ignores the fact that latencies are also clustered by word.
mod_wrong <- lmer(naming_latency ~ frequency + (1 | participant), data = df_crossed)

# Model B: Fully crossed random intercepts for both sampling units.
mod_crossed_int <- lmer(
  naming_latency ~ frequency + (1 | participant) + (1 | word),
  data = df_crossed
)

# Model C: Adds a random slope for frequency within participants on top of the
# crossed intercepts -- our "maximal" model for this design.
mod_crossed_max <- lmer(
  naming_latency ~ frequency + (1 + frequency | participant) + (1 | word),
  data = df_crossed
)
```

Let's directly compare the standard error on the `frequency` effect across these three
models, since that's the number the language-as-fixed-effect fallacy is really about:

```{r compare-se}
cat("Model A (participant only):        SE =",
    round(summary(mod_wrong)$coefficients["frequencyLow","Std. Error"], 1), "\n")
cat("Model B (crossed intercepts):      SE =",
    round(summary(mod_crossed_int)$coefficients["frequencyLow","Std. Error"], 1), "\n")
cat("Model C (crossed + random slope):  SE =",
    round(summary(mod_crossed_max)$coefficients["frequencyLow","Std. Error"], 1), "\n")
```

This is the "language-as-fixed-effect" fallacy made concrete: Model A's standard 
error is roughly a **quarter** the size of Models B and C's, purely because it 
never gave the model a chance to recognize that all 32 participants' 
"Low-frequency" latencies are clustered around the same 20 specific pictures
(and likewise for "High-frequency"). Model A is treating $32 \times 20 = 640$ Low-frequency
trials as though they were 640 independent data points about the frequency effect, when in
fact they only really tell you about 20 independent pictures' worth of information at the item
level. A clinical researcher relying on Model A would report a tighter confidence interval 
and a smaller $p$-value than the data can actually support, purely as an artifact of
ignoring which 20 pictures happened to make it into this particular protocol.

```{r full-summary}
summary(mod_crossed_max)
```

## 4. Partitioning Variance: Intra-Class Correlations

A natural follow-up question in a clinical sample is: how much of the total variance in
naming latency is attributable to *who* the participant is (their overall severity), versus
*which* picture it is? This is answered with an intra-class correlation (ICC) computed from
the variance components.

**A caveat before we do this.** ICCs are cleanly defined for a **random-intercepts-only**
model, where "total variance" is just the sum of each grouping factor's intercept variance
plus the residual. Once a model includes a random *slope* (like `mod_crossed_max` above), the
total between-participant variance is no longer a single number -- it actually differs by
frequency condition, since it depends on the slope variance and the intercept-slope
covariance as well as the intercept variance. For a clean, single-number ICC, we'll compute it
from `mod_crossed_int` (the intercepts-only model) instead:

```{r compute-icc}
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod_crossed_int))
vc

total_var <- sum(vc$vcov)
icc_participant <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "participant"] / total_var
icc_word        <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "word"] / total_var

cat("Participant ICC:", round(icc_participant, 3), "\n")
cat("Word ICC:", round(icc_word, 3), "\n")
```

Here, which person you are accounts for the largest share of the variance (as we'd
clinically expect - aphasia severity varies substantially across people), but the specific
pictures used still account for an important share too - confirmation
that ignoring the word-level variance, as Model A did, would be throwing away a real and
meaningful source of dependency in the data, not a negligible one.

## 5. Syntax Reference for Crossed Random-Effects Structures

For quick reference, here are the `lme4` formula patterns that come up most often for crossed
designs like this one (this block is for reference only -it isn't meant to be run on its
own - and mirrors the explanation in the companion paper):

```{r syntax-reference, eval=FALSE}
# Fully crossed random intercepts (Model B above)
(1 | participant) + (1 | word)

# Crossed intercepts, with a random slope for frequency within participants only
# (Model C above) - note that the random slope is nested under participant, not word,
# because frequency is something that VARIES WITHIN each participant (they name both
# High- and Low-frequency pictures) but is CONSTANT WITHIN each word (a given picture's
# name is always High- or always Low-frequency for everyone who sees it). A random slope
# for frequency within word would not even be estimable here, because frequency doesn't
# vary within a word.
(1 + frequency | participant) + (1 | word)

# The same model, with the random intercept and slope for participant forced to be
# uncorrelated (a "zero-correlation" or parsimonious model, in the sense discussed
# in Section 3, Part 5.3)
(1 | participant) + (0 + frequency | participant) + (1 | word)
# ...or equivalently, using the double-bar shorthand:
(1 + frequency || participant) + (1 | word)
```

The comment on the second block is worth pausing on, because it's the single most common
mistake once designs get crossed: a random slope is only *meaningful* (and only *estimable*)
for a factor that actually varies *within* the grouping unit it's nested under. `frequency`
varies within participants here (each participant names both High- and Low-frequency
pictures), so `(1 + frequency | participant)` makes sense; it does *not* vary within words (a
word's frequency category never changes), so `(1 + frequency | word)` would be asking `lme4`
to estimate something that structurally cannot exist in this design, and it will fail or
return a degenerate result. This is the same general principle we saw in the linguistic
crossed-effects example in the companion paper: "a random slope will be allowable if the slope
factor varies within a cluster of observations... [and] would not be allowable if the slope
factor varies between clusters of observations."

## 6. The Same Logic in Health-Professions Education

Everything above transfers directly to the DPT-assessment scenario mentioned at the start of
this section, just with different names for the same two crossed sampling units:

```{r dpt-analogy, eval=FALSE}
# Confrontation naming:      naming_latency ~ frequency + (1|participant) + (1|word)
# DPT written exam:          exam_score     ~ cohort    + (1|student)     + (1|item)
```

If you were comparing two cohorts of DPT students on a 40-item written exam (say, a "flipped
classroom" cohort versus a traditional-lecture cohort), the 40 specific items on that exam are
a sample from a much larger universe of items you could have written to test the same content
domain. A model with only `(1|student)` implicitly treats those 40 items as if they
*exhausted* the content domain, exactly as Model A did above for the 20 specific pictures --
and would similarly risk reporting a cohort difference with more confidence than the data
actually support. Including `(1|item)` (and, if you have reason to think some students'
cohort-effect is itself variable across items, `(1 + cohort | student)`) is the same fix, for
the same underlying reason.



## Summary

* Whenever participants respond to a *sample* of items (words, pictures, exam questions,
  perturbation trials), treat those items as a random effect, not a fixed one - averaging
  over them or ignoring them entirely can dramatically understate your true standard errors,
  in exactly the way we saw with the frequency effect above.
* A random slope only makes sense for a factor nested under a grouping unit if that factor
  actually varies *within* that unit; a condition that is fixed at the item level (like a
  picture's frequency category, or an exam question's difficulty tier) cannot have a
  meaningful random slope by item.
* ICCs (and "total variance") are only cleanly defined for random-intercepts-only models;
  compute them from the intercepts-only version of your model, not from a model that also has
  random slopes.
* This same crossed structure -- `(1 | participant) + (1 | item)` - applies equally to
  speech-language stimuli, DPT exam items, or any other design
  where participants respond to a sampled set of measurement units.

## References
Clark, H. H. (1973). The language-as-fixed-effect fallacy: A critique of language statistics
in psychological research. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 12*(4), 335-359.
https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(73)80014-3

Judd, C. M., Westfall, J., & Yarkoni, T. (2012). Treating stimuli as a random factor in social
psychology: A new and comprehensive solution to a pervasive but largely ignored problem.
*Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103*(1), 54-69.
https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028347
